label: English Language: set 3 (sentences, punctuation and vocabulary)

papers.title: Phrases and Clauses: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on phrases and clauses, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of these groups of words is a clause?
questions.explanation:
A clause has its own subject and finite verb: *the bell* (subject) *rang* (verb). The others are phrases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- after the long break: This has no verb: it is a phrase (a preposition and a noun group).
- in the school library: This has no subject or verb: it is a prepositional phrase.
- running across the field: *Running* is not a finite verb and there is no subject, so this is a phrase.

questions.stem: Which of these groups of words is a phrase, not a clause?
questions.explanation:
*Under the mango tree* has no subject and no finite verb: it is a phrase. Each of the others contains a subject and a finite verb, so each is a clause.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- when the rain stopped: *The rain stopped* has a subject and a finite verb, so this is a clause.
- because he was late: *He was* is a subject and a finite verb, so this is a clause.
- that she would come: *She would come* is a subject and a finite verb, so this is a clause.

questions.stem:
What is the grammatical name of the clause in bold?

I know **that she will pass the examination**.
questions.explanation:
The clause answers *I know what?* It does the job of a noun (the object of *know*), so it is a noun clause.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- adjectival clause: An adjectival clause describes a noun. This clause is the object of *know*.
- adverbial clause of time: It does not tell us when anything happens.
- main clause: It cannot stand alone as a sentence: it begins with *that* and depends on *I know*.

questions.stem:
What is the grammatical name of the clause in bold?

The boy **who won the debate prize** is my cousin.
questions.explanation:
The clause tells us **which** boy, so it describes the noun *boy*: an adjectival (relative) clause.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- noun clause: A noun clause does the job of a noun. This one describes the noun *boy*.
- adverbial clause of reason: It does not give a reason; it tells us which boy.
- main clause: It begins with *who* and cannot stand alone as a sentence.

questions.stem:
What is the grammatical name of the clause in bold?

We stayed at home **because it was raining heavily**.
questions.explanation:
The clause answers *why did we stay at home?* Clauses beginning with *because*, *as* or *since* (meaning *because*) are adverbial clauses of reason.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- adverbial clause of time: It does not say when; it says why.
- adjectival clause: It does not describe a noun.
- noun clause: It is not the subject or object of a verb; it explains why we stayed.

papers.title: Sentence Types: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on sentence types, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
What type of sentence is this?

*Musa ran to the shop, but it was already closed.*
questions.explanation:
Two independent clauses (*Musa ran to the shop* / *it was already closed*) joined by the coordinating conjunction *but* make a compound sentence.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simple sentence: A simple sentence has only one clause. This has two.
- complex sentence: A complex sentence has a dependent clause. Here both clauses can stand alone.
- compound-complex sentence: There is no dependent clause, so it is not compound-complex.

questions.stem:
What type of sentence is this?

*Although she was tired, Hawa finished her homework.*
questions.explanation:
One main clause (*Hawa finished her homework*) plus one dependent clause (*Although she was tired*) makes a complex sentence.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simple sentence: A simple sentence has only one clause. This has two.
- compound sentence: A compound sentence joins clauses that can each stand alone. *Although she was tired* cannot.
- compound-complex sentence: There is only one main clause, so it is not compound-complex.

questions.stem:
What type of sentence is this?

*The pupils in the front row clapped loudly.*
questions.explanation:
One subject (*the pupils in the front row*) and one finite verb (*clapped*): a single clause, so a simple sentence. *In the front row* is only a phrase.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- compound sentence: There is only one clause; nothing is joined by *and*, *but* or *or*.
- complex sentence: There is no dependent clause.
- compound-complex sentence: There is only one clause.

questions.stem:
What is the function of this sentence?

*Close the door quietly.*
questions.explanation:
A sentence that gives an order, request or instruction is imperative. The subject (*you*) is understood.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- declarative: A declarative sentence makes a statement. This gives an order.
- interrogative: An interrogative sentence asks a question.
- exclamatory: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling, as in *What a lovely day!*

questions.stem:
What type of sentence is this?

*When the rain stopped, we went outside, and the children played football.*
questions.explanation:
Two main clauses (*we went outside* / *the children played football*) plus a dependent clause (*When the rain stopped*) make a compound-complex sentence.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simple sentence: There are three clauses, not one.
- compound sentence: A compound sentence has no dependent clause, but *When the rain stopped* is dependent.
- complex sentence: A complex sentence has one main clause. This has two, joined by *and*.

papers.title: Punctuation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on punctuation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation:
*Its* (no apostrophe) shows possession, like *his* and *hers*. *It's* is short for *it is* or *it has*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The school has it's own borehole.  
  *It's* means *it is* or *it has*. The possessive *its* has no apostrophe.
- The school has its' own borehole.  
  There is no such form as *its'*.
- The school has its own, borehole.  
  No comma is needed between *own* and the noun it describes.

options.label: A
options.content: The school has it's own borehole.

options.label: B
options.content: The school has its' own borehole.

options.label: C
options.content: The school has its own borehole.

options.label: D
options.content: The school has its own, borehole.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation:
A colon introduces a list after a complete clause, and commas separate the items: *Bring the following items: a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bring the following items; a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.  
  A semicolon joins two complete clauses. To introduce a list, use a colon.
- Bring the following items: a ruler a pencil and an eraser.  
  Items in a list are separated by commas.
- Bring, the following items: a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.  
  No comma is needed between the verb *bring* and its object.

options.label: A
options.content: Bring the following items; a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.

options.label: B
options.content: Bring the following items: a ruler a pencil and an eraser.

options.label: C
options.content: Bring, the following items: a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.

options.label: D
options.content: Bring the following items: a ruler, a pencil and an eraser.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation:
Direct speech goes inside quotation marks, and when the reporting words follow, the spoken words end with a comma inside the closing mark.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- "We will win the match" said the captain.  
  When the spoken words come first, a comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
- "We will win the match." said the captain.  
  A full stop would end the sentence too early. Use a comma before *said*.
- We will win the match, "said the captain.": Only the words actually spoken go inside the quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.content: "We will win the match," said the captain.

options.label: B
options.content: "We will win the match" said the captain.

options.label: C
options.content: "We will win the match." said the captain.

options.label: D
options.content: We will win the match, "said the captain."

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation:
Two closely related complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon: *It was getting late; we decided to go home.* (Or: *It was getting late, so we decided to go home.*)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It was getting late, we decided to go home.  
  A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences (a comma splice).
- It was getting late; and we decided to go home.  
  Use either a semicolon or a comma with *and*, not a semicolon with *and*.
- It was getting late we decided to go home.  
  Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation (a run-on sentence).

options.label: A
options.content: It was getting late, we decided to go home.

options.label: B
options.content: It was getting late; we decided to go home.

options.label: C
options.content: It was getting late; and we decided to go home.

options.label: D
options.content: It was getting late we decided to go home.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation:
A reported (indirect) question is not itself a question: it takes statement word order and a full stop.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- She asked me where the library was?  
  A reported question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.
- She asked me, where the library was.  
  No comma is needed before a reported question.
- She asked me where was the library?  
  A reported question uses statement word order (*where the library was*) and a full stop.

options.label: A
options.content: She asked me where the library was?

options.label: B
options.content: She asked me, where the library was.

options.label: C
options.content: She asked me where the library was.

options.label: D
options.content: She asked me where was the library?

papers.title: Homonyms and Homophones: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on homonyms and homophones, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The bride walked slowly down the ____ of the church.
questions.explanation:
*Aisle* (the passage between rows of seats) and *isle* (an island) are homophones: same sound, different spelling and meaning.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- isle: An *isle* is an island. It sounds the same as *aisle* but means something different.
- I'll: *I'll* is short for *I will*.
- ail: *Ail* means to trouble or make ill, as in *what ails you?*

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

We could not ____ the teacher because of the noise from the road.
questions.explanation:
*Hear* (with your ear) and *here* (this place) are homophones. A useful reminder: you **hear** with your **ear**.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- here: *Here* means *in this place*. It sounds like *hear* but is not a verb.
- hair: *Hair* grows on the head.
- hare: A *hare* is an animal like a large rabbit.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mariama wants to buy a new ____ of sandals for the wedding.
questions.explanation:
*Pair* (two things that go together), *pear* (a fruit) and *pare* (to trim) all sound the same.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pear: A *pear* is a fruit.
- pare: To *pare* means to cut away the outer layer, as in *pare a mango*.
- pairs: After *a new*, the noun is singular: *a pair of sandals*.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word *bank* mean the side of a river?
questions.explanation:
*Bank* is a homonym: one spelling with several meanings. Watching canoes go by puts us at the side of a river.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- My father keeps his savings in the bank.  
  Here *bank* means a place that keeps money.
- You can bank on Sahr to help you.  
  Here *bank on* means to rely on.
- The pilot had to bank the plane to the left.  
  Here *bank* means to tilt an aircraft when turning.

options.label: A
options.content: My father keeps his savings in the bank.

options.label: B
options.content: You can bank on Sahr to help you.

options.label: C
options.content: We sat on the bank and watched the canoes go by.

options.label: D
options.content: The pilot had to bank the plane to the left.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The soldiers marched ____ the town at dawn.
questions.explanation:
*Through* (from one side to the other) and *threw* (past of *throw*) are homophones. Use the full spelling *through* in examinations.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- threw: *Threw* is the past tense of *throw*.
- thru: *Thru* is an informal spelling and is not accepted in formal or examination English.
- though: *Though* means *although*; it does not show movement.

papers.title: Figures of Speech: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on figures of speech, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Which figure of speech is used in this sentence?

*The classroom was as quiet as a graveyard.*
questions.explanation:
A simile compares two different things using *like* or *as*: *as quiet as a graveyard*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- metaphor: A metaphor says one thing **is** another. This uses *as… as* to compare.
- personification: Nothing here is given human qualities.
- hyperbole: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration; the key feature here is the comparison with *as*.

questions.stem:
Which figure of speech is used in this sentence?

*The wind whispered through the palm trees.*
questions.explanation:
Personification gives human qualities or actions to things that are not human: the wind *whispered*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simile: There is no comparison with *like* or *as*.
- metaphor: The wind is not said to **be** something else; it is given a human action.
- alliteration: Alliteration is the repetition of the same first sound, which is not the point here.

questions.stem:
Which figure of speech is used in this sentence?

*I have told you a million times to shut that door!*
questions.explanation:
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect: nobody has really said it *a million times*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simile: There is no comparison with *like* or *as*.
- irony: Irony says the opposite of what is meant. The speaker means *many times*, exaggerated.
- personification: Nothing is given human qualities.

questions.stem:
Which figure of speech is used in this sentence?

*Our principal is a lion when pupils break the rules.*
questions.explanation:
A metaphor says one thing **is** another to show a shared quality, without *like* or *as*: the principal is fierce, like a lion.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simile: A simile would use *like* or *as* (*like a lion*). This says he **is** a lion.
- personification: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things; here a person is compared to an animal.
- euphemism: A euphemism is a gentle word for something unpleasant.

questions.stem:
Which figure of speech is used in this sentence?

*Fatu found five fresh fish at the fishing wharf.*
questions.explanation:
Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in words close together: *Fatu found five fresh fish… fishing*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- simile: There is no comparison with *like* or *as*.
- metaphor: Nothing is said to **be** something else.
- hyperbole: There is no exaggeration.

papers.title: Word Formation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on word formation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Without a ladder, it was ____ for Sorie to reach the top shelf.
questions.explanation:
The negative prefix *in-* changes to *im-* before *p*, *b* and *m*: *impossible*, *imbalance*, *immature*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- unpossible: *Possible* does not take *un-*; its negative is *impossible*.
- inpossible: Before *p*, the prefix *in-* becomes *im-*: *impossible*.
- dispossible: *Dis-* does not combine with *possible*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The principal's ____ to close the school early was announced at assembly.
questions.explanation:
The noun formed from the verb *decide* is *decision* (like *divide* → *division*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decidement: *-ment* does not attach to *decide*. The noun is *decision*.
- decition: The noun is spelt with *-sion*: *decision*.
- decided: *Decided* is a verb form or adjective. After *the principal's* we need a noun.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The judge was praised for her ____ in a difficult case.
questions.explanation:
The suffix *-ness* turns many adjectives into nouns: *fair* → *fairness*, *kind* → *kindness*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- fairly: *Fairly* is an adverb. After *her* we need a noun.
- unfair: *Unfair* is an adjective, and it gives the opposite meaning.
- fairment: There is no such word; the noun from *fair* uses *-ness*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The teacher asked Abu to ____ his essay because it had too many mistakes.
questions.explanation:
The prefix *re-* means *again*: *rewrite*, *redo*, *reconsider*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- prewrite: *Pre-* means *before*. Abu must write it **again**.
- miswrite: *Mis-* means *wrongly*; the teacher wants it written again, correctly.
- unwrite: *Un-* reverses an action; you cannot *unwrite* an essay.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Swimming in the river during the rainy season can be very ____.
questions.explanation:
The suffix *-ous* forms adjectives from some nouns: *danger* → *dangerous*, *fame* → *famous*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dangerful: *Danger* takes *-ous*, not *-ful*, to form the adjective.
- dangerly: *-ly* usually forms adverbs, and there is no word *dangerly*.
- endanger: *Endanger* is a verb (to put in danger). After *very* we need an adjective.

papers.title: Vocabulary in Context: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on vocabulary in context, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used in the sentence.

The village was **isolated** after the bridge collapsed, so food had to be carried in on foot.
questions.explanation:
The clue is *food had to be carried in on foot*: with no bridge, the village was cut off.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- crowded with people: Nothing in the sentence suggests crowds.
- completely destroyed: The bridge collapsed, but the village itself was not destroyed: food was still carried in.
- very large: *Isolated* is not about size.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used in the sentence.

The rule is **mandatory**: every pupil must wear the full school uniform.
questions.explanation:
The clue is *must*: a mandatory rule is one that has to be obeyed, that is, compulsory.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- optional: *Optional* means you may choose. The sentence says pupils *must*.
- new: Nothing in the sentence says when the rule was made.
- unpopular: The sentence says nothing about what pupils think of the rule.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used in the sentence.

After weeks without rain, the **parched** fields cracked in the sun.
questions.explanation:
The clues are *weeks without rain* and *cracked in the sun*: *parched* means very dry.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- flooded: *Weeks without rain* means the opposite of flooded.
- green: Fields that crack in the sun after weeks without rain are not green and fresh.
- newly ploughed: The sentence is about the lack of rain, not ploughing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used in the sentence.

The witness gave such a **vague** description that the police could not identify the thief.
questions.explanation:
The clue is that the police *could not identify the thief*: the description was unclear and lacking detail.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- detailed: A detailed description would have helped the police, but they could not identify the thief.
- truthful: *Vague* is about how clear something is, not whether it is true.
- long: *Vague* is not about length.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in bold as it is used in the sentence.

Despite his **meagre** salary, the teacher bought books for his poorest pupils.
questions.explanation:
*Despite* shows a contrast with his kindness: his salary was meagre, that is, very small.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- generous: *Despite* signals a contrast: a generous salary would not need *despite*.
- regular: *Meagre* is about how much, not how often.
- late: *Meagre* is about amount, not timing.
